extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys and applicants working on AI-related inventions before the JPO and CNIPA
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patentability (eligibility, novelty, inventive step, enablement/support, claim drafting) of AI-related and software-related inventions at the JPO and CNIPA. Focuses on how algorithmic and business-method features are treated alongside technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art means any technology known to the public before the date of filing in China or abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline for novelty and inventive step comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty — identical inventions or utility models
rubrics_metrics.description: If the technical fields, technical problems to be solved, technical solutions, and their expected effects are substantially the same between the application and prior art, they shall be regarded as identical inventions or utility models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner compares the application being examined with relevant prior art to determine substantial sameness across these four aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty — separate comparison (no combining for novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining novelty, the examiner shall compare each claim of the application separately with the relevant technical contents disclosed in each item of the prior art, rather than with a combination of the contents disclosed in several items of the prior art or with a combination of several technical solutions disclosed in one reference document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty assessment uses single-item comparisons; combining disclosures is not appropriate for novelty rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty for claims with algorithmic or business-method features
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining the novelty of an invention application containing algorithmic features or features of rules and methods for business, all the features described in the claims shall be considered. The said all the features include both technical features, and algorithmic features or features of rules and methods for business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore algorithmic or business features when assessing novelty; treat the claimed feature set as whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO — claim specification and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner specifies the claimed invention based on the claim, taking the description, drawings and common general knowledge at the time of filing into consideration in interpreting the meanings of words in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should always consider the matter or terms described in the claims and should not ignore them; interpretation uses claim text plus description/drawings/common general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO — approach to software/AI inventions (as a whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: An AI-related invention that also falls under a software-related invention is examined based on the examination method for software-related inventions. When specifying a software-related invention, it is appropriate to understand an invention as a whole, while it is not appropriate to specify it by dividing it into arbitrary arrangements or the like and systemisation methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid artificially dissecting software inventions into isolated parts; treat the claimed invention holistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO — no distinction between technical and non-technical features for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: At the JPO, during the inventive step assessment, no distinction is made between features which are technical and those which are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claim features are considered together when assessing inventive step under the JPO procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO — inventive step assessment procedure (primary/secondary prior art and 4-step reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner selects the prior art most suitable for the reasoning (the 'primary prior art') and determines whether it is possible to reason that a person skilled in the art would easily arrive at the claimed invention from the primary prior art by following steps (1)–(4): (1) determine if reasoning is possible using secondary prior art or common general knowledge to cover differences; (2) if impossible, conclude inventive step exists; (3) if possible, comprehensively assess factors supporting inventive step; (4) if after (3) reasoning is impossible, conclude inventive step exists, otherwise conclude it does not involve an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not regard a combination of two or more independent pieces of prior art as the primary prior art; use the primary/secondary framework and the staged reasoning described.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA — inventiveness definition (prominent substantive features and notable progress)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventiveness means that, as compared with the prior art, the invention has prominent substantive features and represents a notable progress. 'Prominent substantive features' means non-obviousness to a person skilled in the art. 'Notable progress' means the invention can produce advantageous technical effect as compared with the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both non-obviousness and comparative technical effect (advantageous technical effect) are part of the CNIPA standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA — three-step obviousness test
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually the following three steps are followed: (1) determining the closest prior art; (2) determining the distinguishing features of the invention and the technical problem actually solved; (3) determining whether or not the claimed invention is obvious to a person skilled in the art starting from the closest prior art and the technical problem actually solved, i.e., whether there exists a technical motivation in the prior art to apply the distinguishing features to the closest prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such a technical motivation exists, the invention is considered obvious and lacks prominent substantive features.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA — circumstances indicating technical motivation in prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usually thought there exists such a technical motivation where: (i) the distinguishing feature is common knowledge; (ii) the distinguishing feature is a technical means related to the closest prior art, such as a technical means disclosed in another part of the same reference document with the same function; (iii) the distinguishing feature is a relevant technical means disclosed in another reference document with the same function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are non-exhaustive examples to justify combining or applying features from prior documents when assessing obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of algorithmic/business features in inventive step — functional interaction rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention application contains both technical features and algorithmic features or features of rules and methods for business, the algorithmic/business features that functionally support each other and have an interaction relationship with the technical features should be considered together with the technical features as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Functionally support each other and have an interaction relationship' means the algorithmic/business features are closely combined with technical features to constitute a technical means to solve a technical problem and obtain corresponding technical effects; examiners must consider contribution of algorithmic features to the technical solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithms tied to computer internal structure or performance are technical
rubrics_metrics.description: If the algorithm in the claim has specific technical relationships with the internal structure of computer systems, realizes improvement of internal performance of computer systems, or improves hardware computing efficiency or execution effects (reducing data storage/transmission, improving hardware processing speed), then algorithmic features shall be considered to functionally support technical features and contribute to the technical solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such algorithmic contributions should be factored into inventiveness assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business-method features requiring technical adjustments are technical
rubrics_metrics.description: If the implementation of features of rules and methods for business in a claim requires an adjustment or improvement of technical means, then the business-method features and the technical features functionally support each other and their contribution to the technical solution shall be considered in inventiveness examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for required technical modifications as a sign that business-method features contribute technically.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-experience improvements considered when technical
rubrics_metrics.description: If the solution of an invention application brings about an improvement in user experience, and the improvement is brought about or generated by technical features, or by a combination of technical features and algorithmic/business features that functionally interact, it shall be considered in the inventiveness examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements framed as 'user experience' are examinable when they arise from technical contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO — enablement requirement (Article 36(4) JPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must be clear and sufficient to enable any person ordinarily skilled in the art to which the invention pertains to work the invention. The examiner determines the enablement requirement for each claim; if a skilled person cannot understand how to carry out the claimed invention on the basis of the description, drawings and common general technical knowledge at filing, the description is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If carrying out the invention would require trials and errors or complicated experimentation beyond what a skilled person should reasonably be expected to do, enablement is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO — support requirement (Article 36(6)(i) JPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention shall be disclosed in the description. The purpose is to prevent a patent for an invention not disclosed to the public; the examiner determines whether the statements in the claims satisfy the support requirement by comparing the claimed invention and the invention stated in the description, examining substantial correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial correspondence centers on whether a skilled person would recognize that the problem to be solved would be actually solved by the disclosure; claims that exceed the extent of disclosure fail support requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO — violation type: generic claim with only specific embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation exists where a claim is directed to a generic concept but embodiments only of a part of more specific concepts encompassed by the generic concept are stated in the description in a manner that only the specific concepts can be carried out, and there is a well-founded reason that other specific concepts encompassed are not clearly/sufficiently enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both conditions (i) generic claim/only specific embodiments, and (ii) well-founded reason that other variants are not enabled, must apply to find this enablement violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO — AI training-data disclosure condition
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions using training data containing multiple types of data for machine learning, it is essential that either (a) the description recognizes there is a certain relation such as correlation among the multiple types of data, or (b) it can be presumed such relation exists in view of common general technical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps satisfy description requirements for embodiments using mixed-type training data (see referenced case examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO — product function presumed from AI requires embodiment or substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions of a product presumed to have a certain function because of AI cannot satisfy the description requirements without an embodiment in which evaluation on the function is made using a product actually made, unless an estimation result by AI can be a substitution for an evaluation on a product actually made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evaluation often required when claiming product functionality established via AI inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA — enablement and examples of lack of enablement (Article 26.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description shall set forth the invention in a sufficiently clear and complete manner to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it out. Circumstances where the technical solution is regarded as unable to be carried out include: (1) only a task/assumption or wish/result without technical means; (2) technical means so ambiguous/vague that skilled person cannot implement; (3) technical means but skilled person cannot solve the technical problem using them; (4) one of several means in solution cannot be implemented; (5) concrete technical solution provided but requires experimental evidence to establish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete examples examiners use to find lack of enablement at CNIPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA — claims supported by description and limits on generalization (Article 26.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims shall be supported by the description and define the extent of protection sought clearly and concisely. The technical solution for which protection is sought in each claim shall be a solution that a skilled person can reach directly or by generalization from the contents sufficiently disclosed. Generalization of claims shall not go beyond the scope of contents disclosed in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow generalization to equivalents/obvious variants only where a skilled person can reasonably predict same properties/uses; speculative generalizations whose effects are difficult to determine are not allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA — functional feature and pure functional claim limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A technical feature defined by function in a claim is construed as embracing all means capable of performing the function. Whether such functional definition can be supported by the description shall be examined; if embodiments only show a particular way and a skilled person would not appreciate that other alternative means could perform the function, then embracing other alternative means is not allowed. Pure functional definition is not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the description merely vaguely states alternatives without enabling how they might be used, function-based claiming is disallowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA — drafting requirements for computer-program-related inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Description shall outline the technical solution as a whole, illustrate the concept of design and technical features of the computer program and the mode of exploitation to produce the technical effect. The principal flow chart shall be presented and each step explained in natural language in chronological order. Important parts of source code may be briefly extracted but full source is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If computer-program-related invention changes hardware, include hardware entity structure graphs and describe components and relationships to enable implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNIPA — claims for computer programs and apparatus mapping to program modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of computer-program inventions may be process claims or product/apparatus claims. Claims must be supported by the description and represent the technical solution in its entirety, outlining essential technical features rather than only functions/effects. Where an apparatus claim corresponds step-for-step to program flow, components are regarded as program modules and the apparatus claim is treated as program module architecture rather than entity hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful claim drafting needed to reflect whether claimed components are hardware or program-module abstractions; examiner will treat module-based apparatus claims accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description requirements when algorithmic/business features included (CNIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: When algorithmic features or business-method features functionally support and interact with technical features, the description shall clearly and completely set forth how the technical and algorithmic/business features work together to produce advantageous effects. For algorithms: the abstract algorithm should combine with the specific technical field and define at least one input parameter and related output corresponding to data of the specific field. For business methods: the entire process to solve the technical problem shall be described in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe interactions, inputs/outputs and concrete links to technical field so that skilled person can carry out the combined technical solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for inventions containing algorithmic/business features (CNIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims shall be supported by the description and shall record the technical features, the algorithmic features or features of rules and methods for business that functionally support each other or have an interaction relationship with the technical features, and shall define the extent of patent protection in a clear and concise manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must explicitly include the interacting algorithmic/business features together with the technical features; clarity and concision required.
